reasoning: All 12 edits from both groups are kept. The failure edits (5) come first and keep priority, and the success edits (7) cover separate patterns. The only shared anchor is the 'do not repeat clue words' exception bullet in Rule 4. The failure edit there says to drop the geographic type word ('Roanoke', not 'Roanoke Island'), and the success edit says to keep the head word for scales, wars and quoted type nouns ('Beaufort scale', 'Hundred Years' War', 'South Sea Bubble'). These agree under the existing test of whether a trivia key would accept the bare word. I added a short cross-reference to the geographic edit saying that a type word which is part of the standard name stays (e.g. Long Island), so the two edits read consistently. The 'seen here' guidance in the failure edit (generic singular noun) and the success edit (answer from the textual hooks) apply to different cases and do not conflict. The two success bullets about archive page titles and archive categories are kept as one combined edit. Every target string was checked against the current skill, and nothing touches the protected SLOW_UPDATE block.

edits.target: Never cut a part that identifies the person: keep the regnal numeral of a king or of a play's title character ('Richard III', not 'Richard'; 'Henry V').
edits.content: - Historical figures universally known by one name (ancient Romans and Greeks, other famous single-name figures): answer with that bare name as a trivia key would ('Brutus', 'Cassius', 'Cicero', 'Caesar'). Do not expand it to a full Roman name ('Marcus Junius Brutus') or to a namesake's name. When a passage is titled for one namesake (e.g. 'Lucius Junius Brutus, fl. 510 B.C.') but the sentence that matches the clue (a date such as '44 B.C.', an office, a deed) describes a different person, the clue's dates and deeds decide. The bare shared name is then the safest answer, and a different namesake's full name is wrong.

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - Geographic type words: when the clue says 'this island / this river / this lake / this city / these mountains', the clue already supplies the type noun, so drop it if the bare name is the standard answer. 'Philip Amadas & Arthur Barlowe explored this island' -> 'Roanoke' (not 'Roanoke Island'). 'Lake Placid ... in these mountains' -> 'the Adirondacks' (not 'Adirondack Mountains'). For ranges, use the plural short name people say (Adirondacks, Rockies, Alps), not 'X Mountains'. Keep the type word only when it is part of the standard name and the bare word would not be accepted (e.g. 'Long Island', 'Rhode Island').

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Match the number the clue's pointer implies. 'species of these', 'types of these', 'these <plural noun>' or a clue where several different things share the answer ('X & Y had species of these as mascots') -> PLURAL ('Bears', not 'bear'). 'this <noun>', 'one of these' or a single described item -> singular. When the clue says 'seen here' (an image we cannot see), answer with the generic singular noun for the item that the passages tie to the clue's exact action or detail ('Hostess Cupcakes ... split in half' -> 'cupcake'), not simply the brand item mentioned most often.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- The category noun fixes the answer's type. 'this war / battle / treaty / event' -> the NAME of that event (e.g. 'World War II'), never a general, statesman or place that merely appears in a passage. If the passages only reproduce the clue (archive page with the answer cut off) and no passage names the event, answer from your own knowledge using the clue's superlative or unique fact ('material cost greater than all other wars put together' -> 'World War II'). Do not grab a name from an unrelated passage.
- Quoted fragment such as '"...on my mind"': the answer is the MISSING word(s) that complete the famous title or phrase ('Georgia' for 'Georgia on My Mind'). It is never the performer, author or the page's title ('Ellie Goulding'). When passages show several completions (Annie, Georgia, Always, Rhythm), prefer the best-known classic standard, as a one-word proper noun, over a recent single or obscure title.

## Rule 5: Special clue types
- Spoonerism clues (they mention Dr./Rev. Spooner or a garbled phrase like 'queer old dean'): the answer is the INTENDED, unscrambled phrase with its initial sounds swapped back, given in full ('dear old queen'), not a single word and not the garbled form.
- Superlatives: answer on the exact dimension the clue names. 'Smallest in size' (diameter, area, physical size) is not 'smallest denomination/value', and 'largest by area' is not 'largest by population'. If the passages discuss only the other dimension (e.g. 'smallest denomination' = the cent), use common knowledge for the asked dimension (the dime is the smallest U.S. coin in size). Check the candidate against that dimension before answering.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- A clue that is just ONE proper place name ('Timonium') asks for the larger place that contains it (US state, or country for a non-US town). Passages about shops, gyms, schools, fairs or hotels there are only search hits for the name, so never answer with a topic word from them. Pick the state or country the passages attach to the place (Lutherville-Timonium, Maryland -> 'Maryland').
- Picture-reference clues ('The dipper seen here', 'shown here', 'this item pictured') come from a video or image clue you cannot see. Ignore the missing picture and answer from the textual hooks that remain: the related noun in the clue plus the passages that pair it with a single partner ('honey dipper' -> 'honey' for 'used with this sticky substance'). Do not answer with a different sense of the same word (Big Dipper, a character named Dipper).
- Parenthetical stage directions that describe a video or audio clue ('(Jon of the Clue Crew peers down between the cymbals.)') are decoration; answer from the factual part after them. A telegraphic clue with no 'this' ('Georgia guy, flag-fashioning pop painter') defines a person or thing: match EACH descriptor (birthplace, famous work, movement) against the passages and answer with the full name of the one entity that fits all of them ('Jasper Johns').

edits.target: Answer with only that missing word. If a bare number appears in parentheses, treat it only as this hint, not as part of the question.
edits.content: - 'In titles it preceded A's "X" & B's "Y"' / 'it follows ...' / 'this word comes before ...': the answer is ONE word that completes EVERY listed title ('Endless Nights' + 'Endless Summer Nights' -> 'Endless'). Search the passages for each full title and take the word they share. Archive category hints such as 'ROCK "E"' give the answer's first letter or theme, so use them to confirm the candidate. Answer with just that word, not the full titles.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: - The same holds for a clue that describes a famous scene, kiss, quote or event and names the actors or people in it ('Burt Lancaster & Deborah Kerr kiss in the pounding surf'). The slot is the WORK or event they are tied to ('From Here To Eternity'), not one of the named people. Take the title the passages repeat next to those names and that scene, in its standard form.

edits.target: Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content:
- The CATEGORY text in an archive line is part of the puzzle. Many answers are puns or idioms tied to it (category 'WEATHER WORDS & PHRASES', clue 'W. has this type of job' -> 'high pressure'). If the archived answer looks odd as a literal reading of the clue, still trust it and copy it exactly. Do not replace it with a more literal guess from other passages.
- Aggregator and trivia pages often put the answer in the PAGE TITLE while the snippet repeats the clue verbatim: '[TLE] fall - Search-ID.com [PAR] ...a classic of this season; It follows pit, prat & rain...' -> 'Fall'; '[TLE] history - Search-ID.com [PAR] Need help in this subject... Call up Clio' -> 'History'. When a short page title sits on a snippet that contains the clue's distinctive words, treat that title word as the prime candidate and sanity-check it against the clue. Even when the snippet shows only the clue and category (e.g. 'A MUSE ME: ...'), take the anchor entity in the clue (Clio, Goneril) and answer the entity it points to using the other passages.

edits.target: Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Passages often repeat the clue's sentence but drop the answer (a table row such as 'Contrary to popular belief, the desert is only 30% sand'). Then take the answer from that passage's own header or surrounding paragraph (the Infoplease desert table), or from another passage that quotes the full clue. Scan every passage, including odd ones (newsletter PDFs, search-result pages, quiz sites), because one may contain the whole clue followed by its answer.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - If the archive page shows the clue but no answer (a J! Archive show page that lists clues without responses), anchor on the clue's exact numbers and rare terms and find the non-archive passage that ties them to an entity. '51.5 kilometers' + 'new Olympic event' -> 'Olympic distance ... total of 51.5 kilometers' -> 'triathlon'. Answer with the plain generic name, not a brand, series or sponsor name from the passages ('5150 Series').

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content:
- Scales, measures, wars and similar named things keep their head word when the clue supplies only a generic type noun: 'this standard wind scale' -> 'Beaufort scale' (bare 'Beaufort' is incomplete); 'this 1337-1453 conflict' -> 'Hundred Years' War'. Drop only the descriptive modifiers the clue states ('standard', 'wind', '1337-1453').
- Quoted type noun: when the clue puts the generic noun itself in quotation marks after 'this' ('In 1720 bad investments in this "bubble" burst the British economy'), the quoted word is the head of a standard proper name that the passages repeat. Answer with the full name ('South Sea Bubble'), not the bare modifier ('South Sea'). This is the same head-noun exception, not an echo error.
